title: Karmic tail 6-8-20 in the destiny matrix: love in the dock

seo.title: Karmic tail 6-8-20 in the destiny matrix: love on trial
seo.description: 6-8-20 is the karmic tail in which a choice of the heart goes on trial. The Lovers, Justice and Judgement, the family-shame legend, a date check and a way out.

short: The karmic tail 6-8-20 is The Lovers at the entry, Justice as the mechanism and Judgement at the root. Its scenario is a single one: a choice made by the heart never stays just a choice. It opens a court hearing — who is right, who is to blame, was it deserved, what will the family say — and the hearing drags on for years, because scales cannot weigh love. The root card, meanwhile, speaks of a different kind of judgement: not a verdict, but a trumpet that wakes a person from within.

sections.h2: Why 6-8-20 is called "Shame of the Family"
paragraphs: In Russian-speaking destiny matrix circles the tail has two folk names: "Shame of the Family" (Pozor semyi) and "Disappointment of the Lineage" (Razocharovanie roda). The legend behind them is roughly the same. In a past life the soul put its love above its duty to the family, broke the family's order or betrayed it — and became an outcast. The break with the lineage supposedly cost the descendants their support and blessing, and now the person pays for that old deed: with grudges against relatives, with waiting for recognition, with the feeling that their choice will never be approved.

There is no way to verify the legend. Numbers say nothing about past lives, and the tarot books behind the meanings of the arcana know nothing of the matrix or of tails. But the name does not rest on the legend alone. Open the divinatory lists of Arthur Edward Waite, the author of the classic tarot deck and of the key book that goes with it, and the three cards of the tail turn out to speak the language of a single institution. It is the language of the court.

For Justice, Waite writes: "Equity, rightness, probity, executive; triumph of the deserving side in law." Reversed: "Law in all its departments, legal complications, bigotry, bias, excessive severity." For Judgement the first words are "Change of position, renewal, outcome", but right after them: "Another account specifies total loss though lawsuit." And the reversed list of Judgement ends with words that read like a court transcript: deliberation, decision, sentence.

Even The Lovers do not stay out of it. Their upright meaning in Waite is "Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome." In English a trial is both an ordeal and a court case. Waite almost certainly meant the first, but the language itself hints at where this tail is heading. His reversed Lovers read: "marriage frustrated and contrarieties of all kinds." At the entry there is a case about love, in the middle there are scales, at the root there is a sentence.

There is a second piece of evidence — the family. Describing the old form of The Lovers, Waite sees in it **"a card of married life, shewing father and mother, with their child placed between them"**, and adds that the card "is said to have been entitled Simulacrum fidei, the symbol of conjugal faith." Describing Judgement, he speaks of the same people: on the surface it is "the resurrection of that triad—father, mother, child." In Waite's book the same family stands at both ends of the tail. On the first card it comes together; on the last it rises from the grave. The folk legend about the lineage was not made up out of nothing — it was read off the pictures.

Yet Waite himself left a caveat. On his own Judgement card he drew more than three people rising, and he explained exactly why: as "illustrating the insufficiency of current explanations." The family is the surface of the card. What lies underneath becomes clear once we get to the root.

sections.h2: The Lovers at the entry: a choice the heart makes
paragraphs: The first card of the tail sits at point M, where the scenario starts. It is the first reaction at the moment a situation becomes truly personal. In the 6-8-20 tail that reaction is attraction: a person, a cause, a city, a way of life suddenly becomes "mine", and the decision is made before the mind has had its say.

Point M has a feature that is easy to miss. It opens two routes at once: the karmic tail M → N → D and the relationship line M → R1 → R. So everyone with 6-8-20 also has The Lovers at the start of the relationship line. **The door to love and the door to the karmic loop are the same door here** — which is why the tail switches on most often in close relationships.

The two main books describe the card differently, and the difference is useful. Waite writes: "This is in all simplicity the card of human love" — young and innocent, love "before it is contaminated by gross material desire." He deliberately dropped the older picture of a young man standing between vice and virtue, calling it "the later follies". Benebell Wen, author of the modern textbook Holistic Tarot, puts choice at the centre instead. In her words, "in every traditional interpretation of The Lovers, the card is about a moral choice"; the two figures on it are the mind and the heart, and "there is an underlying theme of indecision." She brings in Søren Kierkegaard: "we face an existential choice between two life paths, either one willfully hedonistic or one grounded in our sense of ethical duty."

The tail needs both readings, and they meet at one point: the entry is a choice made by love. Not a calculation and not a compromise, but a pull — exactly what Waite means by "attraction, love, beauty". Marrying someone other than the one the parents had in mind. Leaving the family business for music. Following a person to another city. Or staying — choosing family over love, which is also a choice of the heart, only in the other direction.

The entry does not decide the side. The tail does not say a person will choose love over duty or duty over love. It says something else: **whichever side a person chooses, a hearing follows the choice**.

sections.h2: Justice as the mechanism: scales for what cannot be weighed
paragraphs: The second card sits at point N, the mechanism that keeps the pattern going even after a person has understood everything about themselves. Here it is Justice: the sword and the scales.

Wen herself draws the line between the first two cards. "The Lovers is about making an ethical decision that involves the Seeker," she writes. "Justice is about making an ethical decision that involves an external condition, others who matter to the Seeker, or a situation outside of the Seeker." That is exactly the step this tail takes: a choice "about me" turns into a case "about everyone". In walk the parents, the former partner, the children, an aunt from another city — everyone the choice has touched.

Wen also stresses what kind of court this is: "it is human-created justice, not divine justice. The laws of man are at play." Waite goes further and states what could be called the key to the whole tail. The moral principle "which deals unto every man according to his works" differs in its essence from spiritual gifts — from the capacity for "dedication to the highest things", from the gifts of the poet: "we have them or have not, and their presence is as much a mystery as their absence." And he concludes: "The law of Justice is not however involved by either alternative."

Love is not a wage, and a calling is not a bonus. They cannot go on the scales, because they are not handed out according to works. Yet that is exactly what the mechanism of 6-8-20 does: it carries a choice of the heart to the place where things are counted. Is this fair to the others? Is this happiness deserved? Who is to blame that things turned out this way? What will people think? Every new fact becomes evidence, every conversation a hearing. **The hearing cannot end, because the scales are weighing something that has no weight.** Of the three "court" words in reversed Judgement, the first one rules here — deliberation: the verdict is postponed forever.

In this court a person has two roles and moves easily between them. The defendant — when they spend years proving they had the right to choose, or serve a sentence of guilt. The judge — when they pass sentence on others: on parents who did not understand, on a partner who "owes", on a family that disappointed. The reversed list of Justice warns where the second role leads: "bigotry, bias, excessive severity." Severity towards oneself is severity too.

The mechanism holds for one more reason: it has a throne. Everyone with the 6-8-20 tail has The Emperor at the centre of the chart; that is how the arithmetic works, and no other number can sit at the centre with this tail. Wen sums up The Emperor briefly: "the domination of the mind over the heart"; "All is in order, under control." The staging is precise. At the entry, a choice between mind and heart; in the comfort zone, a mind used to ruling; in the middle of the tail, a court where that mind presides. Wen notices something else as well: on her Emperor card "the kingdom is parched", a sign of "a thirst for a different kind of sovereignty" than the one already attained. There is order but no water — and what can quench that kingdom is only what stands at the root. Even in Manipura, the chakra of will and status, everyone with 6-8-20 has the same cards: two Emperors and Justice, 4-4-8.

sections.h2: Judgement at the root: a trumpet, not a verdict
paragraphs: The third card sits at point D, the root that the whole sequence keeps returning to. Here it is Judgement. Popular readings turn it into the card of the lineage: ancestors, family programs, debts of past generations. As shown above, Waite gives some grounds for this reading — the family rising from the grave — and a caveat against it.

Waite himself sees something else in the card. Judgement, he writes, "registers the accomplishment of the great work of transformation in answer to the summons of the Supernal—which summons is heard and answered from within." And he asks a question worth reading slowly: **"What is that within us which does sound a trumpet and all that is lower in our nature rises in response—almost in a moment, almost in the twinkling of an eye?"**

In Waite's divinatory list Judgement has two faces. One is "Change of position, renewal, outcome." The other, reversed, is "deliberation, decision, sentence." There are no reversed cards in the destiny matrix: a calculated number cannot land upside down. So both faces belong to the same card, and the only question is which one a person lives by. The tail lives by the second — judgement as an endless wait for the verdict. The root asks for the first: hear the call and rise.

Benebell Wen writes a line about Judgement that sounds like a direct reply to "Shame of the Family": "The Seeker's past, no matter how dark, no matter what the Seeker has done, is now behind her or him." For her Judgement is a card of awakening, not of punishment. She accepts the literal sense of judgement too: "All evidence has been made available to the Seeker and the Seeker has rendered his or her judgment." Then she adds: "It does not end there, however." The decision is not the end of the case but the start of a realisation.

Hence the root task of the tail, as we read it: **to leave the courtroom for the call**. To stop waiting for an acquittal — from the family, from a partner, from oneself ten years ago — and to answer the question the choice once asked: what is calling now? On Waite's card the dead rise from their tombs. In life, what rises is whatever was buried under the weight of the trial: the joy of the choice once made, a postponed calling, the right to love without justifying it.

sections.h2: Three stages on one road: Kierkegaard and the engagement ring
paragraphs: Wen mentions Kierkegaard in her description of The Lovers, and that trail is worth following to the end. The Danish philosopher described three stages on life's way. The aesthetic — living by experience, attraction, the beauty of the moment. The ethical — living by duty and by a choice one answers for. The religious — living before the eternal. The 6-8-20 tail repeats them in the same order: The Lovers are attraction and beauty, Justice is duty and the scales, Judgement is a call from above heard from within. The comparison is ours; neither Kierkegaard nor Wen made it. But it would be hard to find a closer picture of the mechanism than Kierkegaard's own life.

On 8 September 1840 Kierkegaard, aged twenty-seven, proposed to eighteen-year-old Regine Olsen, and she said yes. Less than a year later, on 11 August 1841, he sent back the ring with a farewell letter. Regine resisted, and he tried to make her stop loving him on her own by playing a cold scoundrel. On 11 October the break became final. Copenhagen was outraged, and Kierkegaard left for Berlin.

Then came the trial he conducted for the rest of his life. In 1843 he published Either/Or. Its first part holds the papers of an aesthete who lives for the moment, including "The Seducer's Diary". The second consists of letters from his opponent — and Kierkegaard made that opponent a judge: Assessor Wilhelm, known in English as Judge William. The judge writes on "the aesthetic validity of marriage" and on "the balance between the aesthetic and the ethical in the development of the personality". The Danish title uses the word Ligevægten — literally "equal weight". In Danish vægt means both weight and scales; the constellation Libra is called Vægten. The judge's central thesis: an aesthetic choice is no choice at all; a real choice is always ethical.

In 1845 came Stages on Life's Way. Inside is a story whose title sounds like a question put to a jury: **"Guilty?"/"Not Guilty?"**. It is the diary of a man who breaks off his engagement by pretending to be cold; in the story the diary is found in a box at the bottom of a lake. The two question marks in the title are the whole mechanism in miniature: a trial without a verdict.

Regine married someone else. Kierkegaard never married, and in his will he wrote: "It is naturally my will that my former fiancée, Mrs Regine Schlegel, should inherit unconditionally what little I leave behind… for me an engagement was and is just as binding as a marriage." She declined the inheritance. And the diamonds from the engagement ring Kierkegaard had once had reset in the shape of a cross.

A ring turned into a cross is an almost literal drawing of the tail: The Lovers turning into Judgement. Only the road between them ran through a hearing that lasted years. An honest caveat: by Kierkegaard's birth date, 5 May 1813, the same formula gives a different tail. His story proves nothing about people with 6-8-20. It shows what this loop looks like when a person goes all the way round it.

There is also a mirror story, with the choice made the other way. Tolstoy wrote a novel about a woman who chose love against family and duty and was judged for it by everyone: society, her husband, herself. Above the novel he set the epigraph "Vengeance is mine; I will repay" — words from the Epistle to the Romans saying that retribution does not belong to people. Kierkegaard gave up love and judged himself. Anna Karenina chose love, and others judged her. Tolstoy's epigraph draws the same line as the 6-8-20 tail: between human Justice and a Judgement that is not ours to pass.

sections.h2: How the 6-8-20 loop plays out in life
paragraphs: The scenario is recognised not by events but by its course: a choice, then a hearing, then a wait for the verdict — and a new choice that again ends up on trial. The scenery changes; the course stays the same.

paragraphs.h3: In a couple: minutes instead of a date

paragraphs: A person with this tail often chooses a partner with the heart — quickly, warmly, without long calculation. Six months later the couple has an accounts department: who called first, who gives in more often, who put more into the holiday. A quarrel becomes a hearing with exhibits ("and last time you…"), a reconciliation becomes a settlement with conditions. The partner came for a date and found themselves in a courtroom.

After a break-up the hearing goes on alone. Who was right, where the mistake was, could it have gone differently — the case is reviewed for years, and every new romance begins with a secret test: will the choice be vindicated this time?

paragraphs.h3: In the family: a jury of relatives

paragraphs: A choice that goes against the family's expectations — a marriage, a profession, a move, turning down the family business — opens a long trial. The person either files appeal after appeal, proving they did the right thing, or quietly serves a sentence, feeling like the very "shame of the family".

The reverse role exists too. The person becomes the family judge: relatives come to them to settle which sister is right in a quarrel, whether the bride is good enough, whether the country house was divided fairly. "Disappointment of the Lineage" works both ways: one can disappoint one's own people — or be disappointed in them and keep sentencing them for years.

paragraphs.h3: In work: the right to what one loves has to be earned

paragraphs: Here the tail speaks in the voice of "earn it first". Doing what one is drawn to can wait until every obligation has been met. A gift of fate — luck, recognition, easy money — arouses suspicion: what is this for? Fairness at work becomes an obsession: who got promoted, who got more, was the bonus split honestly. The score is kept correctly while life goes by, because in Waite a calling belongs to the order of gifts that are not handed out for merit.

paragraphs.h3: Inside: a trial with no statute of limitations

paragraphs: The quietest form of it comes at night. An old choice returns, and a retrial begins: witnesses, arguments, counter-arguments. The decision was made ten years ago, the consequences arrived long ago, and the case is still open. Wen calls the undertone of The Lovers "an underlying theme of indecision", and here it shows up in a strange way: the choice was made long ago, yet the person still cannot bring themselves to make it.

sections.h2: The price: what the tail takes if it goes unnoticed
paragraphs: The first price is poisoned joy. The choice has been made, the beloved is close, the life's work has been found — but there is no rejoicing until the verdict is read. For The Lovers Wen recalls the old saying "under every flower a serpent coiled", a warning of how quickly bliss can become tragedy. In the 6-8-20 tail the serpent is the suspicion that the happiness was obtained unlawfully.

The second is paralysis of choice. If every decision of the heart ends in years of proceedings, it is easier not to decide: to delay, to wait until others or circumstances decide. But a choice handed over to others is still a choice, and later it too ends up on trial.

The third is severity. Someone who has judged themselves for years sooner or later starts judging others, and by the same merciless standards. It is no accident that Waite put these words in the reversed list of Justice: bigotry, bias, excessive severity.

The fourth is a call that never sounds. While the hearing is in session, no trumpet can be heard. The calling for whose sake Judgement stands at the root is postponed until the verdict, and the verdict never comes.

If guilt becomes unbearable, gets in the way of sleeping and living, and thoughts turn towards self-harm, that is a reason to reach out to a psychologist or psychotherapist right away, and in danger to call your local emergency number or a local crisis line. Reading the tail is a language for observing oneself, not a substitute for help.

sections.h2: How to leave the courtroom: eight practices
paragraphs: The tail cannot be cancelled, and there is no "bad card" to pull out of it: The Lovers, Justice and Judgement are each a resource in themselves. The task is to put every card back in its place: choice belongs to the heart, the scales to what can really be weighed, and Judgement to the call, not the verdict.

ol: **Write down the ruling on the case.** Once, on paper: what was chosen, why, what it cost and whom it affected. The case now has a written decision, and no new hearing is scheduled without new facts.
**Set a statute of limitations.** For an old choice, a date after which the case is closed. When the mind reopens the file at night, it gets a short answer: "closed on the first of March."

**First "I want", then "is it fair".** In a new choice, first name honestly what the heart wants, and only then weigh the consequences. The Lovers are the entry, Justice the next step — not a censor at the door.
**Do not put on the robe in other people's disputes.** When relatives ask for a ruling, listen — and pass no sentence. The role of family judge feeds the same mechanism.

**A conversation instead of minutes.** In a couple, instead of keeping score of who owes whom, name the need: "what I am missing is…". Keep the scales for matters where resources really are being divided.
**Accept without earning.** A gift, a compliment, help — accept it and do not pay it back at once. Gifts, as Waite puts it, we have or have not; they are not handed out according to works.

**Separate guilt from responsibility.** Guilt looks back and waits for punishment. Responsibility looks forward and asks what can be put right. If the choice hurt someone, apologise and fix what can be fixed, rather than serving a sentence.
**Answer the call without waiting for an acquittal.** Once a week, one step towards what calls: a class, a conversation, an application, a trip. Judgement at the root is a response, not a permission.

paragraphs: The sign that the loop has loosened is simple: **the choice stops needing a justification**. A person can say "I decided so" — without a "because" and without waiting for a verdict.

sections.h2: The strong version of 6-8-20: to choose and not to judge
paragraphs: The strong version of the tail is a person who chooses in earnest. Their love is not an accident but a decision they stand behind. The old Latin name of The Lovers that Waite cites — Simulacrum fidei, "the symbol of conjugal faith" — suits them better than any nickname about shame.

Such a person can judge fairly, because they have been through the court themselves and know its cost. People come to them for a fair word: they become mediators, lawyers, editors, mentors, keepers of peace in the family. But their strength is not in verdicts. They know where the territory of the scales ends, and they do not weigh love, talent or someone else's choice.

And they know how to rise. Judgement at the root is a card of renewal: "Change of position, renewal, outcome." Whoever has once walked out of a trial that lasted years knows that the past really can be left behind. Waite mentions an old reading of the figures on The Lovers — **"Truth, Honour and Love"**. He took it for "the gloss of a commentator moralizing", yet admitted: "It has these, but it has other and higher aspects." No formula fits the strong version of 6-8-20 better: love that needs no justification, honour that does not harden into severity, and truth that wakes rather than punishes.

sections.h2: How to check for the 6-8-20 tail by date of birth
paragraphs: The 6-8-20 tail appears exactly when the three numbers of the birth date add up to 20. Here is how to count:

ol: A is the day of birth. If it is greater than 22, add its digits: 28 → 10, 30 → 3.
B is the number of the month.
C is the sum of the digits of the year; if it is greater than 22, add the digits again: 1995 → 24 → 6.
If A + B + C = 20, the tail is 6-8-20.

paragraphs: Example: 28.04.1995. A = 10, B = 4, C = 6, total 20. Everything else falls into place:

The 20 at the root is never the result of reduction: the three numbers of the date have to add up to exactly 20. From there it works as a "plus two" at every step: The Emperor (4) → The Lovers (6) → Justice (8). The whole tail, together with the centre of the chart, grows from a single number.
This arithmetic yields facts that are the same for everyone with 6-8-20:

ul: the centre of the chart is always The Emperor, and Manipura is always 4-4-8;
the relationship line always starts with The Lovers;
people born on the 18th, 19th, 20th, 21st or 22nd never have this tail: the day alone leaves too little room for the month and the year;
people born in 1990–1993 (and also in 1981–1984, 1972–1975 and 1963–1966) never have it either: the year number there is 19–22, and the total inevitably jumps past 20;
from 1994 on, the tail is possible in any year.

paragraphs: How many such people are there? We went through every date from 1 January 1900 to 5 October 2026 — 46,299 days. The 6-8-20 tail comes out on 1,141 of them, 2.46%: fifteenth place out of the 26 possible tails. But generations differ. Among people born in 1960–1999 it is 2.5%, while among those born in 2000–2025 it is already 5%, one in twenty and eighth place.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: Calculation: the classic destiny matrix scheme. The tail is written as M–N–D, where D = A + B + C, the centre E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M, and sums above 22 are reduced by adding their digits. Frequencies come from running every date through the site's calculator.

Arthur Edward Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910; 1922 edition): card symbolism in Part II, divinatory meanings in Part III, the history of the images in Part I. Quotations are from the original.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), chapter 9: The Lovers, Justice, Judgement, The Emperor. Quotations are from the original.
Søren Kierkegaard: Either/Or (1843), Stages on Life's Way (1845); engagement dates and the text of the will are taken from published biographies.
Leo Tolstoy, Anna Karenina, the epigraph.
The link between the three positions, the comparison with Kierkegaard's stages and the practices are the author's interpretation. Waite and Wen do not describe the destiny matrix or karmic tails.

paragraphs: For a couple, 6-8-20 is the task of choosing each other while keeping a voice of one’s own alongside two families. Here the Lovers are the entry to the task, Justice is its middle, and Judgement is the main task: the influence of relatives and the boundaries of the relationship.

faq.q: Is it true that the 6-8-20 tail means "shame of the family" and guilt before one's lineage?
faq.a: There is no basis for that. The legend about a past life in which someone betrayed their lineage for love cannot be checked in any way: numbers say nothing about past incarnations. The cards of the tail describe not guilt but a mechanism — the habit of putting a choice of the heart on trial. The only support the legend has is in the images: the family on Waite's old Lovers and on his Judgement. **The tail passes no sentence** — it shows where a person is waiting for one.

faq.q: Why do I have 6-8-20 both in the karmic tail and in the relationship line?
faq.a: Both lines start at the same point M, so everyone with this tail has The Lovers at the start of the relationship line. A full match of 6-8-20 in both lines happens when the year number is 10 and the day and month also add up to 10 — for example, 07.03.2008. This is the case for roughly one in fifteen people with the tail. Then the same scenario describes both the karmic loop and the way of building a couple, and working with it pays off most in relationships.

faq.q: Why is the 6-8-20 tail twice as common among children as among their parents?
faq.a: Because of the year number. In 1990–1993 it was 19–22, so the 6-8-20 tail could not occur at all; in other years of the last century it also often left little room. After 2000 the year number became small — from 2 to 12 — and the day and month reach 20 far more often. That is why among people born in 2000–2025 one in twenty has 6-8-20, while among those born in 1960–1999 it is one in forty. This is calendar arithmetic, not a sign of a special destiny for a generation.

faq.q: Are the 6-8-20 tail and the "20-8-6 program" the same thing?
faq.a: No. In a karmic tail the order is fixed by the formula: M is the entry, N the mechanism, D the root, and the numbers cannot be rearranged. The calculator never produces 20-8-6 in the tail position; under that name, searches turn up programs from other places in the chart and from other schools. If a reading shows 20-8-6, it is worth asking which line it refers to and not carrying over the description of this tail.

It shares Justice as the mechanism with 15-8-11, but there the entry is The Devil: the scales serve the outburst and pass a verdict that justifies the blow. In 6-8-20 it is love that goes on the scales, and the defendant is often the person and their own choice. With 6-20-14 it shares The Lovers at the entry and Judgement, but there Judgement is the mechanism and the root is Temperance, the card of inner balance. In 6-8-20 Judgement is the root task itself.

faq.q: Does 6-8-20 mean divorce, lawsuits or a break with the family?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events: no lawsuits, no divorces, no family rows. The courtroom words in Waite's lists are an image of the mechanism: the choice is put under review. For one person it is an inner trial nobody around them sees, for another a hard conversation with their parents, for a third it is barely noticeable. **The calculation describes a possible scenario; it does not assign a fate.**

There is no ritual that cancels a tail, and the numbers of a birth date do not change. What changes is something else: the scenario stops switching on by itself. The signs are that a choice of the heart no longer needs a justification, old cases are no longer reopened at night, and the question "what is calling" gets an action rather than another hearing.

faq.q: What if a child has the 6-8-20 tail?
faq.a: Do not tell the child the legend about the "shame of the family": a label easily becomes the first verdict. It helps more to give the child the right to small choices without justification — clothes, an after-school club, a friend — not to hold inquiries of the "and why did you decide that" kind, and not to make the child a judge in adult disputes. In discipline, separate guilt from responsibility: not "you are bad" but "what shall we put right now". That way the mechanism of the tail gets less to feed on from early childhood.

faq.q: Is the 6-8-20 tail different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Sex plays no part in the calculation and does not change the numbers, so the tail and its scenario are the same. Only the scenery differs: whom exactly a person fears disappointing and whose judgement weighs more for them. The course itself — a choice of the heart, proceedings, waiting for a verdict — does not depend on sex.

faq.q: Why is 8 Justice here, when in tarot books 8 is Strength?
faq.a: The destiny matrix uses the old Marseille numbering, in which 8 is Justice and 11 is Strength. Waite swapped these two cards in his deck and says so himself in his description of Strength, which is why books on his deck list Justice as number XI. The meaning of the card does not change: it rests on the name and the image — the scales and the sword.

intro: The cards here are numbered as in the destiny matrix and the old Marseille deck: 8 is Justice. In Waite's deck this card is number XI, but the meaning rests on the card's name, not on its number.

report: Copied out of Arthur Waite's book, the divinatory meanings of the three cards of the 6-8-20 tail read like the record of a court hearing. Justice has "triumph of the deserving side in law", and reversed, "legal complications, bigotry, bias, excessive severity". Judgement has "total loss though lawsuit", and its list ends with deliberation, decision, sentence. Even The Lovers carry "trials overcome" — and in English a trial is also a court case.

Folk readings took the same record their own way and named the tail "Shame of the Family" or "Disappointment of the Lineage". The legend says that in a past life the soul put love above its duty to the family and became an outcast. There is no way to verify it: numbers say nothing about past lives. But the family really is in the cards. Describing the old Lovers, Waite sees "a card of married life, shewing father and mother, with their child placed between them"; describing Judgement, "the resurrection of that triad". **The same family stands at both ends of the tail**: on the first card it comes together, on the last it rises from the grave. And Waite himself left a caveat: on his own Judgement card he drew more than three people rising, as "illustrating the insufficiency of current explanations".

report.h3: Scales for what cannot be weighed

report: At the entry of the tail stand The Lovers — a choice made by the heart: a person, a cause, a city suddenly becomes "mine", and the decision is made before the mind has had its say. The same point opens the relationship line, so everyone with 6-8-20 has The Lovers at its start as well. The door to closeness and the door to the karmic loop are one door here.

What happens next, Benebell Wen describes precisely when she compares the first two cards. "The Lovers is about making an ethical decision that involves the Seeker." Justice is about a decision that involves "others who matter to the Seeker". A choice "about me" becomes a case "about everyone": in walk the parents, the former partner, the children, an aunt from another city. Is this fair to the others, is this happiness deserved, who is to blame that things turned out this way.

The key to the mechanism lies in Waite. The moral principle "which deals unto every man according to his works" differs in its essence from spiritual gifts: "we have them or have not". Love is not a wage, and a calling is not a bonus. **The hearing cannot end, because the scales are weighing something that has no weight.** The verdict is postponed, every new fact becomes evidence, every conversation a hearing.

Which side of the choice is taken does not matter. One can marry against the parents' will, or stay with the family instead of love — the hearing opens either way. It has two roles: the defendant, who spends years proving the right to choose or serves a sentence of guilt, and the judge, who passes sentence on relatives and partners. This court has a presiding officer too: everyone with this tail has The Emperor at the centre of the chart — in Wen's words, "the domination of the mind over the heart".

report.h3: The ring that became a cross

report: No life shows this loop more clearly than Søren Kierkegaard's; Wen brings him in precisely in her description of The Lovers. On 8 September 1840 he proposed to Regine Olsen; less than a year later he sent back the ring, and on 11 October 1841 the break became final. Then came a trial that lasted the rest of his life. In the second part of Either/Or the voice of duty belongs to a judge — Assessor Wilhelm, known in English as Judge William, who writes on "the balance between the aesthetic and the ethical"; the Danish word in the title literally means "equal weight". Stages on Life's Way contains a story called **"Guilty?"/"Not Guilty?"** — the diary of a man who breaks off his engagement.

Kierkegaard never married and left Regine what little he had: "for me an engagement was and is just as binding as a marriage." The diamonds from the engagement ring he had reset in the shape of a cross. The Lovers turned into Judgement — but by way of a hearing that lasted years. By his birth date Kierkegaard has a different tail, and his story proves nothing. It shows what this loop looks like when it is walked all the way round.

report.h3: A trumpet instead of a verdict

report: At the root of the tail stands Judgement, and in Waite this card has two faces: "Change of position, renewal, outcome" — and "deliberation, decision, sentence". The tail lives by the second; the root asks for the first. Waite himself saw in Judgement a summons "heard and answered from within", and asked: "What is that within us which does sound a trumpet and all that is lower in our nature rises in response—almost in a moment, almost in the twinkling of an eye?" About the same card Wen writes a line that sounds like a direct reply to "Shame of the Family": "The Seeker's past, no matter how dark, no matter what the Seeker has done, is now behind her or him."

The way out of the loop is to leave the courtroom for the call. Write down the ruling on an old case once and give it a statute of limitations. In a new choice, first name what the heart wants, and only then weigh it. Stay out of the judge's robe in other people's disputes. Learn to accept a gift, help or love without earning it. Separate guilt, which waits for punishment, from responsibility, which asks what can be put right. And once a week take one step towards what calls, without waiting for an acquittal. **The sign that the loop has loosened: the choice stops needing a justification.**

If guilt becomes unbearable and thoughts turn towards self-harm, that is a reason to reach out to a psychologist or psychotherapist right away, and in danger to call a local emergency number or crisis line.

The strong version of the tail is a person who chooses in earnest and does not judge. The old Latin name of The Lovers that Waite cites — Simulacrum fidei, "the symbol of conjugal faith" — suits such a person better than any nickname about shame. They know the cost of a trial and so can judge fairly, but they do not weigh love, talent or someone else's choice. And they know how to rise: Judgement at the root is a card of renewal.
